deep_reading.title: Let Agents Design How They Search: Automatic Interface Optimization for Agentic Search
deep_reading.content:
When an LLM agent searches a document collection, the tools it can use, how the collection is pre-organized, and how the prompt teaches it to use those tools together make up its "search interface". Today's interfaces are hand-designed and generic across collections; DCI (direct corpus interaction), for example, simply gives the agent a terminal and lets it read raw documents with commands like grep and cat. SearchWeaver, from Korea University and KAIST, instead has a coding agent (Claude Code, running Claude Opus 5.5) design the interface. It reads the search agent's full execution logs and per-question scores, works out why searches failed, and ==revises three things at once==: pre-built index files, executable search scripts, and usage instructions for the search agent. It then reruns the agent and checks the score, for 10 rounds. With GPT-5.4-nano as the search agent, accuracy on BrowseComp-Plus rises from DCI's 71.6% to 78.4%, and mean nDCG@10 over four BRIGHT subsets from 45.7 to 55.0; handing the optimized interfaces unchanged to Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite also beats DCI. The conclusions largely hold, but part of the BRIGHT gain comes from a strong retrieval ranking that one baseline lacks, which the main text does not make obvious; it gets its own discussion below.

## 1. The problem: one interface does not fit every collection

Recent agentic search methods all work within a fixed interface. RAG hands the model only the passages a retriever returns; DCI lets the agent read raw documents with terminal commands; DR-DCI first pulls documents into a workspace via dense retrieval and then browses them; RISE (restricted interaction-space retrieval) fences off a restricted workspace and adds model-generated tables of contents and section anchors to documents. Which of these wins depends on the collection: DR-DCI beats DCI on BrowseComp-Plus (73.1% vs 71.6%) but loses on BRIGHT (42.1 vs 45.7); RISE scores 65.0% on BrowseComp-Plus but only 25.9 on BRIGHT. The authors conclude that interfaces should be designed for a specific collection and model, and that this design work can be handed to a coding agent.

The idea follows prompt optimization such as DSPy and harness optimization such as Meta-Harness. The difference is the target: prompt optimizers change only text, Meta-Harness changes the orchestration code around a model, and SearchWeaver changes how the collection the agent faces is organized and which operations it can call.

## 2. Method: a coding agent repeatedly revises the interface

### 2.1 What an interface consists of

A candidate interface has three parts. First, pre-built files: before any question arrives, the whole collection is processed once, for example to build a "title to file path" index reused by every question. Second, executable tools: Python scripts that can call the supplied BM25 and dense retrieval, restrict search to a subdirectory, or combine the agent's document judgments with a retrieval ranking. Third, usage instructions telling the search agent when to use which tool and how to check clues. The three must be designed together: a tool that "merges the agent's judgments into the ranking" needs instructions telling the agent when to read documents and how to pass its judgments to the tool.

A candidate may also replace the search agent's base system prompt and its context-management policy (which decides when earlier tool outputs get truncated or cleared). The search agent's model weights never change.

### 2.2 The optimization loop

Each round, the designer looks at the collection and all previous candidates and writes a new interface; the new interface is run on the optimization questions, returning per-question scores and full execution logs, including which commands were run, what tools returned, and the final answer. Gold document IDs for optimization questions are also given to the designer, helping it distinguish "never found" from "found but not recognized". Every candidate's results are kept for later reference whether or not it improved. After 10 rounds, the interface with the highest mean score on the optimization set is evaluated on the test questions.

Leakage safeguards are in the appendix: a candidate whose files contain optimization question text, question IDs or gold labels is rejected before evaluation, and test question and label files are made unreadable during optimization. The search agent gets at most 300 turns and 30 minutes per question.

![The optimized BrowseComp-Plus interface and one search (paper Figure 1, right half). (a) Interface: a title index titles.tsv and a script scout.py with four commands, search/pages/locate/verify; the instructions say to search the whole question, look at titles, read the source, and check clues one by one; (b) one question: the agent finds candidate King Diamond, opens the page, locates the line for each clue, then confirms Mercyful Fate's founding year on its page.](figs/2610.29250/fig1_interface.png)

## 3. Results

BrowseComp-Plus asks multi-clue questions over a fixed web corpus, hereafter BCP (multi-clue QA benchmark), judged by GPT-4.1, with 30 questions for optimization and 800 for testing. BRIGHT is reasoning-intensive document retrieval; four subsets are used (biology, earth science, economics, robotics), with 213 optimization and 210 test questions in total, scored by nDCG@10. Each collection gets its own optimized interface.

### 3.1 Main results

| Method | BCP accuracy | Biology | Earth | Economics | Robotics | BRIGHT avg |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| DCI | 71.6 | 61.6 | 51.5 | 31.3 | 38.2 | 45.7 |
| Agentic search (dense) | 62.6 | 58.2 | 51.4 | 34.6 | 35.7 | 45.0 |
| Agentic search (BM25) | 47.5 | 48.8 | 41.6 | 30.2 | 35.4 | 39.0 |
| RISE | 65.0 | 34.9 | 29.4 | 17.7 | 21.7 | 25.9 |
| DR-DCI | 73.1 | 54.4 | 43.4 | 31.7 | 39.0 | 42.1 |
| SearchWeaver | **78.4** | **74.6** | **64.6** | **38.3** | **42.4** | **55.0** |

SearchWeaver leads on both benchmarks and all four subsets. With 800 BCP test questions, 6.8 points is about 54 questions, a reliable gap. Each BRIGHT subset has only about 50 test questions, so a few points on one subset deserve caution, but the roughly 13-point gains on biology and earth science are far beyond that noise.

### 3.2 What each collection's interface learned

The appendix shows the final interface for each BRIGHT subset. All four share a skeleton: the agent still searches and reads raw files with the shell, and a final tool merges the agent's judgments with a ready-made dense ranking into the submitted list. They differ in where retrieval enters and how much weight the agent's judgments get. Biology confines search to the question's topic directory and fuses the documents the agent marks with the dense ranking inside that directory. Earth science searches like plain DCI and uses retrieval only for the final ranking. Economics starts from dense candidates, keeps the agent's order and fills remaining slots from the dense ranking. Robotics puts documents the agent grades as answering the question first.

None of these strategies was written in by hand, and they all differ, which is exactly the paper's point that interfaces should be tailored per collection. But they share one thing: ==all four BRIGHT interfaces end up relying on the supplied ReasonEmbed-Qwen3-8B ranking==. The DCI baseline has no dense retrieval at all, the "agentic search (dense)" baseline uses the smaller ReasonEmbed-Qwen3-4B, and DR-DCI uses BGE-large. The paper does not report what that 8B ranking scores on its own without the agent, so the 9.3-point BRIGHT gain cannot be split from the main text into interface design versus stronger retrieval resources.

### 3.3 Is changing the prompt enough?

The next comparison partly answers the question from Section 3.2. Two variants: first, the same loop but only the instructions may change, with no generated files or tools and no retrieval resources; second, SearchWeaver's final interface with its generated files, tools and corresponding instructions removed, without re-optimization.

| Method | BCP | Biology | Earth | Economics | Robotics | BRIGHT avg |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| DCI | 71.6 | 61.6 | 51.5 | 31.3 | 38.2 | 45.7 |
| Prompt optimization only | 75.6 | 71.4 | 56.2 | **41.8** | 38.8 | 52.0 |
| SearchWeaver | **78.4** | **74.6** | **64.6** | 38.3 | **42.4** | **55.0** |
| Files and tools removed | 72.5 | 64.9 | 53.1 | 38.8 | 38.0 | 48.7 |

Changing only the prompt, with no retrieval resources at all, lifts the BRIGHT average from 45.7 to 52.0, about two thirds of the total gain. That means most of the benefit comes from "telling the agent how to search this collection", not from the extra ranking. Only the remaining 3 or so points need files, tools and retrieval resources, and they are concentrated in biology and earth science: removing files and tools costs those two subsets 9.7 and 11.5 points. Economics is slightly higher without them (38.8 vs 38.3), and prompt-only optimization scores best there (41.8). In other words, the toolset optimized for economics did not help; it was selected only because it had the highest mean on the optimization set, which shows that selecting over 10 rounds and a few dozen optimization questions brings in some noise.

### 3.4 Tool time

![Accuracy versus mean tool time (paper Figure 2). The horizontal axis is tool execution time per question (excluding model inference); the vertical axis is BCP accuracy (left) and BRIGHT nDCG@10 (right).](figs/2610.29250/fig2_pareto.png)

The paper stresses that SearchWeaver saves time over DCI: tool execution time per question (excluding model inference) falls from 42.4 s to 32.9 s on BCP and from 63.2 s to 36.6 s on BRIGHT. The appendix breaks it down by subset:

| BRIGHT subset | DCI mean (s) | SearchWeaver mean (s) | DR-DCI mean (s) | RISE mean (s) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Biology | 62.2 | 12.3 | 8.0 | 1.7 |
| Earth science | 78.8 | 63.5 | 9.8 | 2.2 |
| Economics | 43.3 | 26.3 | 10.1 | 1.9 |
| Robotics | 66.6 | 40.7 | 17.2 | 1.7 |

The saving comes mainly from biology, because it restricts search to one topic directory; the earth-science interface keeps DCI's whole-corpus search and saves little. Compared with other methods SearchWeaver is not fast: DR-DCI and RISE use a fraction of its tool time. It trades more tool time than those two for higher scores, so the authors' claim that it sits on the Pareto frontier among the evaluated methods is accurate, but "saves time" holds only relative to DCI. Also, only tool execution time is counted, not model inference time, which in multi-turn interaction may well be the larger share; the paper does not report it.

### 3.5 Does it transfer to another model?

Handing the interfaces optimized with GPT-5.4-nano unchanged to Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite gives 73.9% BCP accuracy (DCI 60.9%) and 58.8 mean BRIGHT nDCG@10 (DCI 50.7), above DCI on all four subsets, with BRIGHT tool time per question falling from 23.1 s to 15.5 s. Working without re-optimization means ==a good part of what was optimized belongs to the collection itself, not to tricks for one model==. Note, though, that with Gemini, RISE and DR-DCI reach 69.1% and 69.6% on BCP, both more than 8 points above DCI; gaps between methods shift a lot with the model, so a ranking under one model should not be taken as settled.

## 4. Limitations

The limitation the authors state is that experiments use fixed collections; when documents are added or changed, when the pre-built index and the tools that depend on it need updating, and whether that can be done incrementally, is not studied.

There are several more. First, optimization cost is not reported. Every round has Claude Opus 5.5 read full execution logs and then reruns the search agent over the optimization set; the call volume and cost over 10 rounds are the numbers anyone adopting the method most needs. Second, BCP optimization uses only 30 questions, and the paper does not analyze overfitting to them; the test gains show there is no severe overfitting, but that may not hold for other collections. Third, retrieval resources on BRIGHT are unequal, as Section 3.2 explains. Fourth, each collection was optimized only once, with no report of variation across seeds or designer models.

## 5. Practical takeaways

For teams building QA agents over an internal knowledge base, this gives a process to copy: prepare a small batch of questions with gold answers, and have a coding agent read the execution logs and revise the prompt, generate index files and write search scripts. The ablation says the cheapest first step is prompt-only optimization: BCP accuracy goes from 71.6% to 75.6%, BRIGHT gets two thirds of the gain, and no extra retrieval resources are needed. If the collection has a clear directory structure or decent dense retrieval, then let the designer build tools that restrict search to relevant directories and combine the agent's judgments with the retrieval ranking. If the collection changes often, you will need to design how the generated index is maintained.

deep_reading.title: MAPS: Macro-Adaptive Parallel Reasoning for Regulating Search Momentum in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
deep_reading.content:
RAG methods that interleave reasoning and retrieval, such as Search-o1, have the LLM write each next sub-query with all previous reasoning and sub-queries in view. This paper from Northeastern University (China) and Tsinghua starts with a measurement: embed each sub-query, accumulate the step-to-step movements with exponential weights into what it calls "search momentum", and test whether that predicts the direction in which the next sub-query deviates from the original question. Prediction gets more accurate at later steps, from which the authors conclude that ==later sub-queries keep drifting along the direction earlier ones already took==. Their method, MAPS (a macro-adaptive parallel reasoning framework), makes two changes: each round the model sees only the retrieved knowledge and a compressed reasoning state, never the earlier sub-queries or full reasoning; and each round it first lists several complementary search directions, writes one sub-query per direction, retrieves in parallel, and merges the results. On Qwen3-32B, MAPS averages 56.0 Cover-EM (whether the gold answer appears in the response) across six QA datasets, against 49.2 for the strongest baseline, ParallelSearch, and 43.9 for Search-o1. The gains are real, but the "search momentum" diagnostic itself has several weak points, discussed below.

## 1. The problem: do sub-queries drift further and further?

Multi-hop questions need evidence scattered across several documents, so the common approach is to have the model write sub-queries as it reasons. The sub-query at step t is conditioned on all earlier reasoning and sub-queries, so one early off-target sub-query can pull every later retrieval off course. The appendix case is typical. The question is which of *La Môme Vert-De-Gris* and *The Pod People* has the earlier-born director. Search-o1's first retrieval finds director Olivier Dahan, but its reasoning then invents a *Pod People* directed by Natasha Lyonne and Amy Nicholson, queries Amy Nicholson's birth date, then drifts to documentary production and 1930s organizations, and ends up querying the membership of the Farm Holiday Association, ever further from the question. MAPS's parallel sub-queries find both directors, Bernard Borderie and Juan Piquer Simón, in the first round and then search only for their birth dates.

### 1.1 How search momentum is computed

The authors embed the original question and each sub-query with E5 to get vectors q_0, q_1, q_2, … and define:

- momentum m_t = β_t·m_{t−1} + (1−β_t)·(q_t − q_{t−1}), i.e. a weighted accumulation of each step's movement, where larger β_t weighs history more;
- alignment S_t = cos(m_t, q_{t+1} − q_0), the cosine between the current momentum and the next sub-query's total offset from the original question.

The fitting data: run Search-o1 (Qwen3-32B) on 1,000 questions each from 2WikiQA, MuSiQue and HotpotQA, keeping only trajectories with at least three retrieval rounds; fit each β_t with L-BFGS-B on the training set to maximize S_t, then report S_t on another 1,000 questions.

papers.title: Signals and Queries: Token-Efficient Agentic Context Discovery
papers.summary: Parlant used to ask an LLM whether each customer-service rule is relevant every turn—about 69,000 tokens for 36 rules. S&Q instead has an LLM offline write 10 triggering user messages and 10 easily confused counterexamples per rule and trains a logistic regressor; online each turn needs one embedding and 37 µs of CPU. On τ²-bench airline support at 90% recall, precision is 32%–34% versus 31% for a cosine threshold; after mining examples from real dialogues precision rises to 43.5%, and ==almost all of that lift comes from the counterexamples==.

deep_reading.content:
Customer-facing LLM agents are usually bound by dozens of behavioral rules, such as "compensate only if the passenger bought travel insurance". Every turn, the agent must first decide which rules apply to the current situation and then put them in the prompt. Parlant's engine used to ask an LLM "is this policy relevant now?" once per policy per turn; with 36 policies that is 36 LLM calls and about 69,000 prompt tokens per turn. The Parlant team's Signals and Queries (S&Q) replaces this step with small classifiers trained offline. For each policy, an LLM writes, offline, 10 user messages that should trigger it and ==10 user messages that look similar but belong to a neighbouring policy==. These are embedded, and a separate logistic regression is fitted for that policy. At run time each turn needs one embedding call and 36 dot products, 37 microseconds of CPU, and the authors estimate per-turn cost is roughly 100,000 times lower than asking an LLM per policy. On 254 conversation states from τ²-bench airline customer service, taking the LLM judge as ground truth, S&Q reaches 32% precision at ≥90% recall with Gemini embeddings and 34% with OpenAI embeddings, only 1 to 3 points above a plain cosine threshold. Switching to exemplars mined from real conversations lifts precision to 43.5% and 41.6%. The paper's real value is not its default numbers but that ==it pins the bottleneck on where the exemplars come from==.

## 1. The problem: missing a rule is an error, an extra rule is just waste

Stuffing every rule into the prompt each turn does not work. Content in the middle of a long context tends to be ignored, attention per instruction gets diluted, adherence drops as instructions pile up, and token cost grows linearly with the number of rules. So the relevant rules have to be filtered first.

The cost of filtering is asymmetric. Miss the cancellation policy and the agent may do something it should have refused; include an irrelevant rule and you spend a few hundred extra tokens. S&Q therefore first guarantees at least 90% recall per rule and only then improves precision. It is a pre-filter: a rule filtered out can never be recovered later, while the surviving rules are read again by the agent's own LLM, which can ignore the irrelevant ones.

The cheapest option is to compare the conversation directly against the rule text by embedding similarity, but it works poorly. Conversations are informal user messages, rules are formal normative prose, and the two separate badly in embedding space. Another approach places different instructions at different nodes of a flow graph so each prompt stays small, but this fragments the agent's behavior and is hard to maintain.

## 2. Method

### 2.1 Offline: positives and hard negatives for each rule

For each rule, gemini-3.5-flash generates two sets of user messages from the rule text alone. The first set is signals, messages that should trigger the rule; for the cancellation policy, "I want to cancel my flight to Chicago next week". The second set is anti-signals, messages on a nearby topic that a different rule should handle, such as "I'd like to move my flight from Tuesday to Thursday", which belongs to the change policy. No real conversations are used in generation.

### 2.2 One logistic regression per rule

For each rule, a logistic regression is fitted on the embeddings of these 20 messages and outputs a probability of relevance. Each rule's classifier depends only on its own exemplars. Adding or editing a rule means generating its exemplars and fitting one classifier (about 2 ms); no other rule is affected.

The authors explain why they do not use other rules' positives as negatives. They tried that early on. Two rules that sit close in embedding space then fall into each other's negative sets, both classifiers push their shared region to the negative side, and a turn that is truly relevant to one of them gets rejected by both. The more rules and near-synonyms there are, the worse this gets. Giving each rule its own negatives removes this mutual suppression by construction.

### 2.3 Online: take the max over two views of the conversation

At turn t, two kinds of vectors are scored and the maximum is taken: the embedding of the whole conversation so far, and the embedding of each individual user message so far. All vectors are centered on the centroid of the rule embeddings and then normalized, and a rule is kept if its score exceeds a global threshold θ. Taking the max over individual user messages keeps an earlier topic from diluting the signal of a later one when the conversation shifts.

![Where points land on one rule's logistic classifier (Cancel flight; paper Figure 2). The x-axis is the classifier score. Green: generated signals; red: generated anti-signals; the two separate cleanly. Blue stars are real conversations the LLM judged relevant, grey crosses those judged irrelevant; both crowd into the middle and overlap heavily. The purple dashed line is the negative threshold set to protect recall.](figs/2610.29326/fig2_logreg.png)

This figure shows the core difficulty of the whole paper. Generated exemplars separate perfectly on the classifier, yet real conversations all land between them, with relevant and irrelevant ones overlapping heavily. To miss as few relevant conversations as possible, the threshold has to go negative (−0.45 for Gemini, −0.4 for OpenAI), and many irrelevant conversations get through as a result. That is the root of the roughly one-third precision: ==there is a clear distribution gap between generated exemplars and real conversations==.

## 3. Experiments

### 3.1 Setup

The data are 50 airline customer-service conversations produced by a Parlant agent against the τ²-bench user simulator. Every prefix ending at a user message is one query state, 254 in total. There are 36 rules: the 6 sections of τ²-bench's airline policy plus 30 written by the authors (identity verification, baggage claims, unaccompanied minors, fare rules, fraud handling and so on), deliberately including several near-synonym clusters. deep_reading.title: A Small Model Asks Better: Fine-Tuning Query Clarification for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
deep_reading.content:
In a multi-turn RAG conversation, two kinds of question should get a clarifying question before an answer. One is a question with an unclear referent: the assistant has just described two credit cards and the user asks "what rewards does this card have?" The other is subtler: the question reads as clear, but the retrieved documents support several answers. Ask "is the language that descended from Common Brittonic still spoken today?" and the documents mention Welsh, Breton and Cornish. IBM Research built ClariEdge, a dataset of about 3,900 examples ==that deliberately includes hard negatives: questions that look ambiguous but whose referent the earlier turns already fix==. They use it to LoRA-tune 3B-scale Granite models so that one small model both decides whether to ask and, when it does, writes a clarification that lists the candidates. Granite-4.1-3B LoRA reaches 96.6% decision accuracy; the best prompted model, GPT-4o, gets 79.4%, and GPT-5.6 Sol only 73.1%. Retrained without hard negatives, accuracy on the hard-negative class falls from 87.3% to 35.4%, which shows that learning when *not* to ask comes mostly from those examples.

![The two cases that need clarification (paper Figure 1). (a) Two cards appear in the dialogue, so "this card" is unclear and the clarification lists the candidates; (b) the question is clear but the documents mention three languages, so the clarification gives a short answer for each.](figs/2610.28686/fig1_examples.png)

## 1. The problem: when to ask, and what to say

Existing datasets each cover only part of this. CLAMBER evaluates isolated single questions with no dialogue history and no retrieved documents. AmbigQA counts a question as ambiguous whenever retrieval surfaces several factual answers, yet for a question like "who controlled the Italian government in 1922?" today's models simply answer "Mussolini and the Fascist Party" with no need to ask. ClariQ and Abg-CoQA have dialogue but do not use retrieval results as evidence. A real RAG assistant has to judge using the dialogue and the documents together.

The hard part is on the other side. Many questions look ambiguous but the earlier turns have already settled them. If the user said "I work at the Northeast branch" and then asks "when does this branch's service open?", "this branch" is unambiguous. A model that asks about these too interrupts the user on every turn, which is worse than an occasional wrong answer. So the core of the task is not "find ambiguous questions" but ==drawing an accurate line between real and apparent ambiguity==. The data design, the ablation and the cross-domain test in the paper all revolve around that line.

## 2. How the dataset is built

### 2.1 Three classes

Conversations come from four domains of MTRAG, IBM's earlier multi-turn RAG benchmark: ClapNQ (Wikipedia), Cloud (technical docs), FiQA (finance) and Govt (government sites). Examples fall into three classes:

| Class | Meaning | Train | Test | Total |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Ambiguous | Really needs a clarifying question | 967 | 104 | 1,071 |
| CLEAR-random | Ordinary clear question, an easy negative | 1,800 | 200 | 2,000 |
| CLEAR-hard | Looks ambiguous but the context settles it | 742 | 79 | 821 |

Ambiguous examples have two sources. First, annotators were given an entity type and its instances (say, "park" with several state parks) and wrote a question that deliberately names none of them, such as "what are the park's opening hours?"; a script then appended it as the last turn of an existing multi-turn conversation. About 75% were attached to conversations on the same topic and about 25% to unrelated ones, simulating a user who suddenly switches topic. The authors then checked each result by hand and dropped cases where the earlier turns happened to name the entity and so removed the ambiguity. Second, Mistral-Large-3 generated questions over 793 conversations, targeting an entity type with several instances in the dialogue; for 228 longer conversations (more than 6 turns, several entity types) it used step-by-step reasoning with self-verification.

### 2.2 Hard negatives come from the generator's mistakes

A good share of the questions from the second route are not actually ambiguous. One appendix example: the assistant has just explained bots, and the user asks "what are their capabilities?"; by coreference "their" can only mean bots. Mistral-Large-3 produced this as an ambiguous question, which shows that ==the generator itself cannot tell where the line is==. The authors reviewed every item: genuinely ambiguous ones went to Ambiguous, ones resolvable from context went to CLEAR-hard. The review also surfaced recurring kinds of apparent ambiguity: comparison questions ("which one has the best battery life?" compares all candidates rather than pointing to one), ordinary follow-ups, and terse keyword queries like "Price?". In effect, CLEAR-hard collects the generator's misjudgments and uses them as a training signal.

Note that hard negatives are built only for the setting without retrieved documents. The post-retrieval setting has no counterpart, so cases like "the documents seem to offer several answers but they can be merged into one reply" are not covered.

### 2.3 Reference clarifications

Each ambiguous example has a reference clarification written in one of three styles by number of candidates: with 2–3 candidates, list each with a one-line answer; with 4–8, list just the names; with too many or no enumerable candidates, simply ask "which X do you mean?". Mistral-Large-3 drafted them and humans corrected them. Two authors independently labeled 80 test examples (20 hard negatives, 40 random, 20 ambiguous) for ambiguity, reaching a Cohen's Kappa of 0.875; all 4 disagreements were in CLEAR-hard, again showing that even people find this line hard.

## 3. Model and deployment

The authors LoRA-tune Granite-4.0-micro, Granite-4.1-3B and GPT-OSS-20B on 3,509 training examples, with rank 32 and α 64 on both attention and MLP layers, on a single H100, for up to 15 epochs with early stopping on the validation set. The input is the dialogue history plus optional retrieved documents; the output is a JSON object: CLEAR (meaning no clarification needed) if the question is clear, otherwise one clarifying question.

![Where the ClariEdge LoRA sits in a RAG pipeline (paper Figure 2). Top: before retrieval it sees only the dialogue and retrieval runs only on CLEAR; bottom: after retrieval it sees dialogue plus documents and the generator runs only on CLEAR.](figs/2610.28686/fig2_deployment.png)

In deployment the same LoRA is used in two places: before retrieval it sees only the dialogue and decides whether to ask first; after retrieval it sees dialogue plus documents and decides whether to ask before generating. That adds at most two small-model calls per turn. A 3B model keeps latency and cost low, and the pre-retrieval check can also save a pointless retrieval.

The baselines are seven prompted models: GPT-5.6 Sol, GPT-4o, GPT-OSS-120B, GPT-OSS-20B, Granite-4.1-30B, Granite-4.1-3B and Granite-4.0-micro. All receive the identical system prompt, which spells out the three clarification styles and the rule to use only information in the context. Because Granite-4.1-3B exists in both a prompted and a LoRA version, the gap between them can be attributed to training rather than model size.

## 4. Results

### 4.1 Whether to ask

| Model | Ambiguous | CLEAR-random | CLEAR-hard | Overall | Pre-retrieval overall | Post-retrieval overall |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Granite-4.1-3B LoRA | 91.3 | 99.5 | 96.2 | **96.6** | 93.0 | 100.0 |
| Granite-4.0-micro LoRA | 84.6 | 98.5 | 87.3 | 92.4 | 85.6 | 99.0 |
| GPT-OSS-20B LoRA | 76.9 | 98.5 | 86.1 | 90.1 | 82.4 | 97.4 |
| GPT-4o | 48.1 | 90.5 | 92.4 | 79.4 | 81.3 | 77.6 |
| GPT-5.6 Sol | 93.3 | 72.5 | 48.1 | 73.1 | 68.4 | 77.6 |
| GPT-OSS-120B | 80.8 | 83.0 | 65.8 | 78.9 | 75.4 | 82.1 |

| Granite-4.1-3B (prompted) | 26.9 | 88.0 | 55.7 | 64.8 | 59.4 | 69.9 |

(%) The most telling part of this table is not the overall score but the fact that prompted models err in two opposite directions. GPT-5.6 Sol and GPT-OSS-20B over-ask: above 90% on Ambiguous but only 48.1% and 58.2% on hard negatives, and they misjudge nearly 30% of ordinary clear questions too, so roughly one in four normal questions gets a clarification. GPT-4o and the small Granite models under-ask: GPT-4o scores 92.4% on hard negatives but only 48.1% on Ambiguous. Two frontier closed models leaning opposite ways shows that this bias does not shrink with scale; the prompt simply does not convey where the line is.

The post-retrieval results make the point sharper. After retrieval GPT-4o gets only 32.6% on Ambiguous: with several answers plainly in the documents, it usually just answers. The two Granite LoRAs reach 100% and 99.0% there. But the post-retrieval subset has no hard negatives, only ambiguous and ordinary clear questions, so those perfect scores come from an easier distribution and should not be compared directly with pre-retrieval ones. Pre-retrieval is the hard part: Granite-4.1-3B LoRA gets only 84.5% on Ambiguous there, because without documents the model has only linguistic cues to separate real ambiguity from a resolvable reference.

### 4.2 Are the listed candidates right?

Clarification quality is measured on candidates: precision is the share of generated candidates that are correct, recall the share of reference candidates covered. Correctness is judged by Llama-3.3-70B with four prompts, and only on examples the model correctly flagged as ambiguous.

| Granite-4.1-3B LoRA | 95/104 | 92.7 | 85.7 | 89.0 |

Second, hard negatives cover only the pre-retrieval setting, so the 100% post-retrieval accuracy is measured on a distribution without them. Third, clarification quality is scored entirely by one LLM, and the paper does not report how well that judge agrees with humans. So the references are reliable; whether the judge is equally reliable is untested. Fourth, the prompted baselines use a single prompt with no few-shot examples or targeted tuning, so part of the over- and under-asking bias might be reduced by a better prompt.

## 6. Practical takeaways

When building a multi-turn RAG assistant, "should I ask?" can be handed to a 3B LoRA called once before and once after retrieval, instead of relying on a large model with a prompt. The main lesson is about data: the training set must contain counterexamples that look ambiguous but are settled by context, and the easiest source of them is to have a large model generate ambiguous questions and then pick out, by hand, the ones it got wrong. If post-retrieval false ambiguity is common in your setting, for example several documents that really say the same thing, you will need to add that kind of hard negative yourself. IBM Research built ClariEdge, a dataset of about 3,900 examples that deliberately includes hard negatives: questions that look ambiguous but whose referent the earlier turns already fix. 1. The problem: when to ask, and what to say

Existing datasets each cover only part of this. CLAMBER evaluates isolated single questions with no dialogue history and no retrieved documents. AmbigQA counts a question as ambiguous whenever retrieval surfaces several factual answers, yet for a question like "who controlled the Italian government in 1922?" today's models simply answer "Mussolini and the Fascist Party" with no need to ask. ClariQ and Abg-CoQA have dialogue but do not use retrieval results as evidence. A real RAG assistant has to judge using the dialogue and the documents together.

The hard part is on the other side. Many questions look ambiguous but the earlier turns have already settled them. If the user said "I work at the Northeast branch" and then asks "when does this branch's service open?", "this branch" is unambiguous. A model that asks about these too interrupts the user on every turn, which is worse than an occasional wrong answer. So the core of the task is not "find ambiguous questions" but drawing an accurate line between real and apparent ambiguity. The data design, the ablation and the cross-domain test in the paper all revolve around that line.

2. How the dataset is built

2.1 Three classes

Conversations come from four domains of MTRAG, IBM's earlier multi-turn RAG benchmark: ClapNQ (Wikipedia), Cloud (technical docs), FiQA (finance) and Govt (government sites). Examples fall into three classes:

Ambiguous examples have two sources. About 75% were attached to conversations on the same topic and about 25% to unrelated ones, simulating a user who suddenly switches topic. The authors then checked each result by hand and dropped cases where the earlier turns happened to name the entity and so removed the ambiguity. Second, Mistral-Large-3 generated questions over 793 conversations, targeting an entity type with several instances in the dialogue; for 228 longer conversations (more than 6 turns, several entity types) it used step-by-step reasoning with self-verification.

2.2 Hard negatives come from the generator's mistakes

A good share of the questions from the second route are not actually ambiguous. One appendix example: the assistant has just explained bots, and the user asks "what are their capabilities?"; by coreference "their" can only mean bots. Mistral-Large-3 produced this as an ambiguous question, which shows that the generator itself cannot tell where the line is. papers.title: Uni-Mem: Learning a Long-Horizon Agentic Memory Manager with Unified Online Policy Optimization
papers.authors: Zhiqian Xia, Jielong Tang, Ling-An Zeng, Shixiong Kai, Rong Yao, Hao Kong, Xiao Dong, Wei Wang, Mingxuan Yuan, Siyu Xia, Haifeng Xia
papers.summary: Huawei Noah and collaborators propose Uni-Mem: one Qwen3-4B-Instruct jointly learns what to write into a memory store and what to fetch at query time, both with online RL. Training alternates write and retrieve optimization, ==holding the other part fixed inside each contrastive group so reward differences come only from the part being trained==; rewards are assigned per "event" (a new dialogue span or a question) to the related memory ops. On LoCoMo the LLM-judge score is 88.80%, 10.93 points above Memory-R2 (OSS), and 80.99% without SFT.

papers.title: How AI agents search
papers.authors: Francesca Pezzuti, Ophir Frieder, Fabrizio Silvestri, Sean MacAvaney, Nicola Tonellotto
papers.summary: The University of Pisa and collaborators release ASQ, about 1.02M full retrieval traces from open search agents (Search-R1, AutoRefine, gpt-oss-20b) on MS MARCO, HotpotQA, and Researchy Questions, including every sub-query, retrieval result, and reasoning text. A question can trigger up to 186 retrievals while people usually search 2–3 times; agents often revisit earlier queries and fetch the same results again; ==adding a reranker or deepening retrieval does not reliably shorten the chain==, and effects vary by agent and setup.

papers.title: BIRD-RL: Scaling Agentic Reinforcement Learning over Stateful Data-Centric Environments
papers.authors: Ge Qu, Jinyang Li, Xiaohan Xu, Xiaolong Li, Bowen Qin, Nan Huo, Ziwei Tang, Chenhao Ma, Reynold Cheng
papers.summary: HKU and collaborators propose BIRD-RL, RL that trains small models to debug SQL on real databases. The hard part is that ==SQL mutates database state, so each sampled trajectory would otherwise need its own database container==; BIRD-RL registers and reuses DB replicas per trajectory, raising space efficiency 12.8× on SQLite without Kubernetes. Training has four stages: imitate reasoning, imitate multi-turn tool use, reinforce reasoning, then interactive RL on real DBs. 7B and 14B models reach 44.40% and 48.00% success on BIRD-CRITIC-SQLite versus 48.20% for Claude-Opus-4.6 Agent.

papers.title: Harness Scaling for Generalizable Agentic Reinforcement Learning
papers.authors: Fei Bai, Huatong Song, Chuan Hao, Ran Tao, Jian Yang, Bryan Dai, Wayne Xin Zhao, Ji-Rong Wen
papers.summary: Renmin University and collaborators find that ==RL inside one fixed agent harness hurts when the model is moved to another harness==. Harness Scaling splits the harness into five swappable parts—system prompt, tool interface, observation format, context management, workflow—picks a small orthogonal set of combinations for training, and pairs each task with two nearby combinations. Training Qwen3-4B-Instruct on ClawGym-Task raises GRPO mean score on unseen harness combinations from 29.81 to 39.04; transfer to Claude Code averages 37.22, above SFT (35.08) or RL (33.38) done directly on OpenClaw.

papers.title: Flint-interactive: A language for creating interactive data visualizations
papers.summary: Microsoft Research releases Flint-interactive so agents can generate interactive charts with click, filter, zoom, and cross-plot linking. Interaction is split in two: a compiler turns raw clicks and drags into semantic events such as "which data the user selected" and applies render updates; ==the agent only writes which event triggers which update== (highlight, annotate, pan/zoom) and never low-level rendering. Use it via Flint-MCP in chat or via a programming API in dashboards and tables. The blog gives no reliability or cost numbers.

papers.title: Inside NVIDIA Sentry: Secure AI Agents at Runtime
papers.summary: NVIDIA describes Sentry, an agent security framework that runs on a BlueField-4 DPU and is ==independent of host software==; all agent traffic to models and the public internet must pass through it. DOCA Tower is a transparent proxy that decrypts traffic and approves requests with Open Policy Agent rules; DOCA Argus reads host memory to check that the requesting process and container hashes are on an allowlist. On anomalies, hardware can isolate the agent in milliseconds, and logs live on the DPU where the agent cannot change them. Launch is planned for early next year; no performance numbers are given.
